patterns.name: Setup, then payoff, in under 15 seconds
patterns.what: Show only the 3–6 s that make the payoff make sense, then the payoff, then 1–2 s of the reaction. No match context, no loading screens. Either start on the setup with a 'watch this' text, or cold-open on the payoff frame and rewind ('wait, how did we get here').
patterns.why_it_works: Completion and rewatches are the top Reels/Shorts signals; a 12 s clip with one clean payoff loops. Viewers only need to understand the stakes, not the game.
examples: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=71DYZLHob7I (Protatomonster, 10 s 'right place at the right time')
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ML0rjNI9WyE (Kevvv FPS, 18 s '1 in a MILLION chance!')

patterns.name: Freeze-frame + meme stinger + 'Bro thought…' caption
patterns.what: Freeze on the frame just before disaster (0.5–1 s, often desaturated or B&W), stamp a caption ('Bro thought he could flash over the wall'), hit one meme sound (record scratch, vine boom), unfreeze into the fail. The 'moments before disaster' grammar.
patterns.why_it_works: The freeze tells the viewer a payoff is coming (open loop) and the caption makes it readable to non-players. One stinger is funny; three are noise.
examples: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JexIOA7IJaM (RICHLEV 'Lil Bro Thinks He In a Edit', 1.05M)
trend: gaming meme-sound edits (brain/research/trends.json id gaming-meme-sound-edits)

patterns.name: Zoom/crop to the moment
patterns.what: Punch in 1.3–2x on the crosshair, kill feed, health bar or the friend's character at the payoff; shake 2–4 frames on impact. In vertical, crop to the action rather than letterboxing the whole 16:9 frame.
patterns.why_it_works: Gameplay is tiny on a phone; zoom shows what matters and doubles as emphasis on the beat.
examples: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g5reb3lTx88 (Hextech Lab Short: tight on the one thing)

patterns.name: Banter is the content: word-timed captions of comms
patterns.what: The friends' voice chat, captioned word by word, carries the joke; the game is the stage. Comms compilations outperform their channels by 10–30x.
patterns.why_it_works: Voices are human and original (nobody else has your friends), and captions make it watchable on mute. Non-players get the joke from the words.

patterns.name: Fails beat wins (clutch vs choke)
patterns.what: The choke, the teamflash, the 0.1 s defuse miss and the self-molotov travel further than the ace. Best of all is a clutch that turns into a choke, or the reverse, with the viewer asked to guess.
patterns.why_it_works: Fails are relatable and shareable ('this is you'); wins are only impressive to people who play at that level.

patterns.name: Rage as a physical beat
patterns.what: A facecam rage moment (scream, head in hands, controlled desk tap) timed to the in-game cause, often with a rage meter or phonk drop.
patterns.why_it_works: Physical reaction translates without game knowledge; it is the most clipped streamer moment (CaseOh/Jynxzi).

patterns.name: Jump-scare reaction cam
patterns.what: Big facecam (top half or full-bleed with game PiP), 1–3 s of tense silence or breathing, the scare, the scream, then the friend laughing. Often a 2-frame black or white flash on the scare.
patterns.why_it_works: Faces sell fear; the laugh after the scream releases tension and makes it loopable and shareable.
examples: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wk6iXvnz2HY (daukey 'try not to giggle in the backrooms', 3.45M)

patterns.name: Co-op chaos: friends as recurring characters
patterns.what: The same 3–5 friends, each with a role (the betrayer, the coward, the one who reads nothing, the hoarder). Titles frame the group ('4 idiots', 'When Idiots Play', 'Dhokebaaz').
patterns.why_it_works: Series and characters drive follows: viewers come back for the people. Co-op physics games (R.E.P.O.) and proximity chat generate unscripted comedy every session.

patterns.name: Numbered series and compilations
patterns.what: 'FUNNIEST MOMENTS #70', 'CURSED WEAPONS #10', 'TOP 100 #7'. Every part trains the audience to expect the next one.
patterns.why_it_works: Series give the best view-to-follower ratio (Brain atom growth-series-view-to-follower). Small channels get outliers from parts deep in a series (EEZGAME #25 805K on 8K subs).

patterns.name: Skit inside the game
patterns.what: A stereotype or a character voice acted over gameplay: 'every bronze Yasuo', 'when a girl joins the lobby', a Punjabi uncle character in Valorant, Discord-chat skits.
patterns.why_it_works: Insiders tag friends ('this is literally you'); skits are original by construction.

patterns.name: Small channels, huge outliers with honest titles
patterns.what: Low-key titles that sound like a friend talking, on clips of their own friend group: 'Backrooms but it's just the moments I found mildly funny'.
patterns.why_it_works: Proof that the algorithm serves good friend-group clips regardless of subscriber count; honesty reads as authentic.

patterns.name: Vertical layouts for 16:9 gameplay
patterns.what: (A) facecam top third, game bottom two-thirds cropped to the action; (B) full-bleed crop on the action with a small round facecam; (C) blurred-fill background with the full 16:9 frame in the middle and captions above/below (for wide moments like LoL teamfights or the minimap); (D) two POVs stacked (my POV vs friend's POV) for betrayals and screams.
patterns.why_it_works: Each layout keeps the payoff large on a phone. Switching layouts at the beat is itself a pattern interrupt.

patterns.name: Ride the release calendar with your own footage
patterns.what: Release and event windows (GTA 6 on Nov 19, MW4 launch, LoL Worlds final Nov 14, game updates) get searched and recommended, but the winners use their own angle: a GTA 6 map in another game, trolling the new game's players.
patterns.why_it_works: Topic demand is high, and the viewer still gets something original.

patterns.name: Originality rules: reuse is now down-ranked
patterns.what: From Oct 1, 2026 YouTube Shorts recommendations reduce reach for re-uploads of others' content without meaningful additions; YouTube's rep said voice-over, minor edits and template bulk changes don't make a clip original. Instagram already excludes reposts and watermarked clips from recommendations.
patterns.why_it_works: Srijan's advantage is that his clips are his own and his friends'. Compilation aggregators (Red Arcade-style) are exactly what's being squeezed.

india_notes: Hinglish banter wins: the biggest Indian gaming channels (Techno Gamerz 53.4M, Total Gaming 45.9M, Live Insaan 15.7M) narrate in Hindi/Hinglish. For Instagram, speak Hinglish and caption in Roman Hinglish (or English captions for wider reach) so non-Hindi viewers can follow.

Indian-server culture is a genre of its own: 'Valorant India is NOT kid friendly', 'Ultimate Mumbai Server Experience', CS2 'Indian lobby' voice chats. Gaali-heavy VC is the joke, but bleep or mute it: reach and brand safety drop with unbleeped abuse.

Mobile (BGMI, Free Fire) dominates mass Indian gaming; PC games (CS2, Valorant, LoL) are a smaller, older, urban audience, which fits a 26-year-old office worker's account better than kid-skewed Minecraft/Roblox Hindi content (ghost-follower risk, Brain atom growth-follower-first-ghosts).

Valorant and Fortnite lead Indian social gaming chatter, with BGMI third (Sprinklr data via storyboard18). CS2 has an active Indian community but few good creators (Salty Boys at 8K subs): the lane is open.

LoL in India is niche (no Indian server; players queue abroad on high ping, our understanding). Make LoL clips universally readable (fails, pings, flame) rather than India-specific, and use English captions for global LoL viewers.

LAN and gaming-cafe culture: 'gaming cafe' visits, ₹25–₹60/hour PC cafes, LAN events (S8UL/BGMI LANs, STANFEST Bengaluru Oct 31) and the 'friends in one room' energy. A Pune cafe session with friends is a cheap way to film reaction cams with consent.
Office-gamer identity: '9–6 job, 11 PM ranked', 'standup call after an all-nighter', corporate English vs gaming rage. This ties gaming to Srijan's corporate-guy positioning and to gym/tech pillars.

Desi reference bank (use as text/voice jokes, not copyrighted clips): Zomato/Swiggy ratings, Pune rent and brokers, Indian dad directions, Maggi at 2 AM, power cuts, chai, 'beta padhai karo', shaadi season, Diwali patakhe (Diwali is Nov 8, 2026). Bollywood dialogue audio is copyrighted: recreate the line in your own voice or use the Instagram library version in-app.
India release calendar for gaming hooks: GTA 6 preload Nov 12 and launch Nov 19 (console only at launch), LoL Worlds final Nov 14, BGMI Survivor League until Nov 17, MW4 launch window now.

research.lane: 'The office guy and his idiot squad': a 26-year-old Pune corporate employee who plays LoL and CS2 after work and loses his mind with the same 3–4 friends in R.E.P.O. and Escape the Backrooms. Not a pro, not a kids' let's-player. Every clip is his own footage, cut tight (setup → payoff in under 20 s), with Hinglish banter captioned word by word, one meme stinger per payoff, and recurring franchises (Worst Teammate of the Week, Bro Thought, Clutch or Choke, Corporate Subtitles). It stacks onto his gym and tech pillars (rig, rank, rage) and stays clear of the reposted-compilation model that YouTube's Oct 2026 originality change punishes.

workflow.detail: Copy all existing clips into one folder tree: Gaming/00_inbox → 01_raw/<game>/ → 02_moments/ → 03_projects/<post-id>/ → 04_exports/ → 99_gold/. Rename raw files as YYYY-MM-DD_game_map-or-mode_people_note.ext, e.g. 2026-10-21_cs2_inferno_srijan-rohit-aman_premier.mkv. Then run a quick audit so you know what each file has (length, resolution, fps, how many audio tracks): for f in 01_raw/*/*; do ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration:stream=index,codec_type,width,height,r_frame_rate -of compact "$f"; done. Files with 2+ audio tracks (game / mic / Discord) are gold: you can caption the banter cleanly.

workflow.do: Find loud moments (screams, laughs, rage) from the audio
workflow.detail: Most funny moments are audio spikes on the mic or Discord track. Measure loudness every 0.1 s: ffmpeg -i clip.mkv -map 0:a:0 -af "aresample=48000,asetnsamples=n=4800,astats=metadata=1:reset=1,ametadata=print:key=lavfi.astats.Overall.RMS_level:file=rms.txt" -f null - (use 0:a:1 or 0:a:2 for the mic/Discord track if it exists). Then list every second that is 12 dB louder than the clip's median, merge spikes closer than 3 s, and pad each by 8 s before and 3 s after (the setup comes before the scream). A 10-line Python loop over rms.txt does this; Claude can run it for a whole folder and write moments.csv.

Volume alone also catches gunfire. earshot's listening transcript tags events with AudioSet classes, including Laughter, Giggle, Screaming, Shout and Gunshot: ~/sm-tools/earshot/.venv/bin/python -m earshot timeline clip.mkv --detail high --json --out tl.json, then keep events tagged Laughter/Screaming/Shout. For one long session, ask directly: earshot find mic.wav "a group of friends laughing loudly" --top 10. Laughter after a spike = a confirmed funny moment.

Extract the voice track (ffmpeg -i clip.mkv -map 0:a:1 -ac 1 -ar 16000 mic.wav) and run faster-whisper with word timestamps: .venv/bin/python tools/transcribe.py mic.wav small (writes mic.wav.words.json). Search the transcript for comedy keywords: 'bhai', 'what', 'no no no', 'kya kar raha', 'bro', 'run', 'bachao', 'sorry', 'gg', laughter. Hinglish caveat: auto-detect often picks Hindi and writes Devanagari; for Roman-script captions rerun with language='en' and hand-fix Hindi words (budget 2–3 min per 30 s clip). The words.json later becomes the captions.

For CS2/Valorant/LoL, crop the kill-feed area and detect when it changes: ffmpeg -i clip.mp4 -vf "crop=iw*0.28:ih*0.22:iw*0.72:0,select='gt(scene,0.08)',showinfo" -f null - 2>&1 | grep -o 'pts_time:[0-9.]*' (CS2 kill feed is top-right; LoL's is right-middle; adjust the crop). Three or more kill-feed changes within 6 s = a multi-kill. OpenCV can do the same plus detect the grey 'you died' screen (mean saturation drops) to find your deaths fast.

Put every candidate in moments.csv: file, start, end, game, people, tag (fail / clutch / choke / betrayal / scream / banter / rage / physics), rating 1–5, used_in. Watch only the shortlisted windows at 1.5x. Keep only 4s and 5s that pass the shareability test: 'who would I send this to, and why?'. Cut them losslessly into 02_moments: ffmpeg -ss 00:12:31 -to 00:12:52 -i clip.mkv -map 0 -c copy 02_moments/2026-10-21_cs2_choke-1v2_r5.mkv (re-encode later in the edit).

Pick a layout per idea. (A) facecam top, game bottom (1080×608 + 1080×1312): ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v]crop=889:1080:515:0,scale=1080:1312[g];[0:v]crop=480:270:0:810,scale=1080:608[f];[f][g]vstack[v]" -map "[v]" -map 0:a -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -r 30 out.mp4 (move the game crop's x to centre the action; the facecam crop assumes a 480×270 cam in the bottom-left). (B) full-bleed action crop: crop=608:1080:X:0,scale=1080:1920 (record at 1440p so the crop stays sharp). (C) blurred fill for wide moments: [0:v]scale=1080:1920:force_original_aspect_ratio=increase,crop=1080:1920,boxblur=20[bg];[0:v]scale=1080:-2[fg];[bg][fg]overlay=(W-w)/2:(H-h)/2. (D) two POVs stacked: each crop=1215:1080:X:0,scale=1080:960, then vstack. In CapCut: Canvas 9:16 → duplicate the clip → crop each copy → keyframe Position to follow the action.

Turn words.json into word-by-word captions (2–4 words on screen, active word highlighted). Fastest on phone: CapCut Auto captions (supports Hindi; check Roman vs Devanagari) and fix words. Local: Claude converts words.json to an .ass subtitle with per-word karaoke highlight and burns it with ffmpeg -vf ass=subs.ass, or HyperFrames renders animated captions. Rules: label who is talking by colour (Srijan white, friend 1 yellow, friend 2 cyan), keep captions in the middle band (above the bottom 350 px and below the top 250 px), bleep and asterisk gaali (b***), and add a translation line in English only when the Hindi joke matters.

One stinger per payoff, never two in a row. Place the stinger on the frame of the payoff (the death, the drop, the scream), duck or cut game audio under it for 0.3–0.6 s, and freeze-frame for 0.5–1 s if the joke needs reading time. Meaning map: record scratch = 'wait, rewind'; vine-boom bass hit = realisation; 'bruh' = disappointment; riser = tension before a scare; cut-to-silence = horror beat. Levels per library/mixing/MIXING.md: meme stings at about voice level, once. Check sync with earshot timeline out.mp4 (offset should be within one frame). Source: earshot's bank for hits/risers/glitches; meme stings must be found (Openverse CC0, or Instagram's in-app sound library).

Banter clips: no music, or a bed at −22 to −24 LUFS that drops out on the punchline. Montages: phonk or trending audio cut to the beat. Instagram: add trending audio inside Edits at 5–15% under the original sound, or use a low-use track. YouTube: use YouTube Audio Library or nothing; copyrighted phonk and game OSTs can be Content-ID claimed. Horror: let the game's silence work; add a sub-drop only on the scare.

Voice/comms −16 LUFS (anchor), game −20 to −24 LUFS under talking and up to −16 when nobody talks, SFX per MIXING.md, final master −14 LUFS integrated, true peak −1 dBTP. If game and voice are on one track, use CapCut's 'Enhance voice' carefully (it can eat the game). Verify with earshot critique export.mp4 --fast.

Meme payoff: 7–15 s (loops). Story clip with banter: 20–35 s. Mini compilation (5–6 moments, ≤8 s each, numbered): 45–60 s. Explainer-skit (court case, real-estate tour): 35–60 s. YouTube Shorts: same cuts, under 60 s. YouTube long: 8–14 min episodes or monthly compilations with chapters. Cut every dead second; a visual change every 1.2–2.5 s.

1080×1920, 30 fps (60 fps if the game motion matters and the clip is 60 fps), H.264 high bitrate, HDR off. Text inside safe zones. Instagram: post from Edits (no watermark), collab-tag friends who appear, 3–5 hashtags, keyword caption. YouTube Shorts: re-export without Instagram text styling if needed, title = hook line. Cover frame = the freeze-frame with the caption.

After posting, move the source moment to 99_gold/<game>/ and fill used_in in moments.csv. Every month, unused 4-rated moments become the YouTube compilation, and the top Reel gets a part 2. Log views, sends and saves per post to see which franchise to double down on.

workflow.do: Capture setup going forward (OBS Studio, free)
workflow.detail: Settings → Output → Advanced → Recording: format Hybrid MP4 or MKV (remux later), encoder NVENC/AMF (HEVC or H.264), rate control CQP 18–20, keyframe 2 s, preset P5. Video: base = your monitor res, output 1920×1080 (or 2560×1440 for crop headroom), 60 fps. Audio tracks: Track 1 = full mix (for quick posts), Track 2 = game (Application Audio Capture → game .exe, or Desktop Audio), Track 3 = mic, Track 4 = Discord (Application Audio Capture → Discord.exe). Tick tracks 1–4 in Recording, assign in Advanced Audio Properties. Replay buffer: Output → Replay Buffer → enable, 90–120 s, set a 'Save Replay' hotkey (e.g. F9) and start the buffer with every session, so you only press a key after something funny happens. Vertical: the Aitum Vertical plugin (needs OBS 31.1+) adds a 1080×1920 canvas with its own 'backtrack' (replay) hotkey; untick 'Use main OBS settings' and pick tracks or vertical files record silent. Facecam: iPhone 15 on the tripod as a webcam (Camo or Iriun app, free tiers) placed bottom-left at 480×270 in the 16:9 scene so the Step-7 crop recipe works. Fallback: NVIDIA App / AMD Adrenalin instant replay (separate mic track option).
